images.caption: Raikoke volcanic island is near the center of the Kuril Islands in the Sea of Okhotsk in the northwest Pacific Ocean. The island is roughly circular with dimensions of 2.0 by 2.5 kilometers. On June 22, the volcano erupted with a gas and ash plume reaching 17 kilometers. The two ASTER images, acquired exactly 10 years apart on June 30, dramatically depict the changes to the island. In 2009, vegetation (red) covered most of the island. The 2019 image shows an ash and steam plume rising from the caldera. There is no trace of any vegetation, ash deposits having buried everything. The images are located at 48.3 degrees north, 153.2 degrees east. (Images prepared by M. Ramsey, U. Pittsburgh)

images.caption: This image takes us to Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula in the northern Pacific, typically covered in bright white clouds on satellite. However, on June 22, 2019, the NOAA/NASA Suomi-NPP satellite caught a different type of cloud poking through—the towering brown ash cloud from the eruption of the Raikoke volcano on Kamchatka’s Kuril Islands. This was the first major eruption of Raikoke since 1924 and it shot about 6-8 miles into the atmosphere. NOAA’s JPSS satellites don’t just track the visible ash plumes of volcanoes, they also have an instrument called the Ozone Mapping Profiler Suite (OMPS), which can track the movement of the sulfur dioxide (SO2) gas released from volcanic eruptions.
